"The meditation practiced by fools, the meditation on the characteristics and meanings of observation,
the meditation on the suchness of objects, and the pure meditation of the Tathāgata."
Like the forms of the sun and moon, like the *padma* lotus, the deep abyss, like space,
and the extinction of fire— thus do practitioners contemplate these various signs:
the external paths and the meditations of common attainment.
Furthermore, they fall into the realms of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Abandoning all of those, there is then nothing whatsoever.
All the Buddhas of all lands, with inconceivable hands,
"At one time, he stroked [the disciple's] crown of the head, and [the disciple] entered accordingly into the mark of suchness (*tathatā-lakṣaṇa*).

For example, like the sun and moon, various signs of dhyāna appear to demonstrate gain and loss; that is to say, within meditative concentration, one may see forms like the sun or moon, or see the *padma*, here translated as the red lotus."
In some instances, one sees the ocean appearing with deep and perilous features;
in others, it is like empty space;
or it is like a fire that has been extinguished, leaving behind only ashes.

In general, when practitioners of contemplation perceive these various signs appearing, they should not grasp at them with attachment; for if they do so, they will fall into the heterodox meditations of external paths or descend into the realms of the two vehicles.
One should observe carefully and relinquish everything; when not seeing even a single dharma that can be apprehended, there is nothing at all, and one may enter the Tathāgata-dhyāna.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
regarding parinirvāṇa, what dharma do you teach when you speak of nirvāṇa?"
“There are three kinds of nirvāṇa:

namely, the falsely conceptualized nirvāṇa of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), the nirvāṇa realized and attained by the followers of the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas), and the ultimate nirvāṇa of the Tathāgata.

Although these three types of nirvāṇa share the same name, they differ greatly in reality. If one does not employ the Dharma to correctly define their names, then the Tathāgatagarbha will be conflated with that of ordinary beings and followers of the two vehicles; thus, it must be distinguished, and for this reason I have posed this question.”
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"The transformation of all self-nature habitual tendencies—the latent impressions of the *ālaya*, the *manas*, and the *manovijñāna*—is called *nirvāṇa*.
The *nirvāṇa* of the Buddhas and myself is the realm of the emptiness of self-nature."

Regarding "the habitual tendencies of the self-nature of all things," the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states, "the habitual tendencies of the self-nature of all consciousnesses. This refers to the portion of habitual tendencies consisting of the mental clinging to the nature of the mind-consciousness of all sentient beings.
The "storehouse," "mind," and "mental consciousness" refer to the ālayavijñāna and the active consciousnesses; these terms denote one's own mind.
The reason all are said to be "habitual tendencies" is that they have been perfumed by the delusive thoughts of craving and views since beginningless time.

Regarding "transformation": it refers to transforming the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) and the object-consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*) into the sphere of the noble wisdom of self-realization; this is called *nirvāṇa*.
However, since all sentient beings are already in the state of *nirvāṇa*, what transformation could there be?
This refers to the transformation of names while the substance remains untransformed.

Regarding "the Buddhas and I": "Buddha" refers to this ultimate *nirvāṇa*. I and the Buddhas have realized it together; there is no separate realization. One simply understands that birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is itself *nirvāṇa*, and even the nature of *nirvāṇa* cannot be apprehended. This is the realm of the reality of emptiness.

"Furthermore, Mahāmati, nirvāṇa is the realm of self-realization through noble wisdom; it is free from the false imaginings of annihilation and permanence, and transcends both existence and non-existence.
Why is it not permanent? "
It is called "non-eternal" because the conceptualization of specific and general characteristics has been severed.
Why is it not "annihilated"?
It is because all noble ones—of the past, future, and present—attain self-awakening; therefore, it is not annihilated.
Because it is free from emotional attachment, it is not eternal; because it reveals the fundamental nature, it is not annihilated.
Mahāmati, nirvāṇa is neither destroyed nor does it die.
If nirvāṇa were subject to death, it would follow that one must undergo rebirth and continuity;
if it were subject to disintegration, it would fall under the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Therefore, nirvāṇa is free from disintegration and free from death; for this reason, it is the refuge of those who practice.
The statement that *nirvāṇa* is neither destroyed nor dead is made in contrast to that which is subject to destruction and death.

This is because *nirvāṇa* is the principle of non-arising and non-ceasing. While ordinary beings are subject to destruction and death, those of the Lesser Vehicle enter the *nirvāṇa* of true emptiness; by extinguishing the body so as to have no body, and extinguishing wisdom so as to have no wisdom, they too may be said to be neither destroyed nor dead.

Although one has departed from birth within the realm of分段 (fen-duan) [limited, fragmented existence], one still undergoes birth through transformation (變易 sheng, *pariṇāma-utpatti*); this is the characteristic of continuity.
Although one has departed from existence, one still clings to emptiness; this is still conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Now, the Tathāgata’s nirvāṇa is free from all these marks; this is the destination for those who practice the Mahāyāna.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati, nirvāṇa is neither abandonment nor attainment, neither annihilation nor permanence, neither a single meaning nor manifold meanings; this is called nirvāṇa."
This section summarizes the preceding meaning.
"Not one" means it is not emptiness; "not manifold" means it is not the provisional. That which is neither empty nor provisional precisely reveals the Middle Way, the Great Nirvana.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati, as for the nirvāṇa of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas:

they perceive self-characteristics and common characteristics; they do not frequent sense objects; they possess non-perverted views; and their conceptual constructions do not arise. Thus, they conceive of that state as nirvāṇa."

The followers of the Two Vehicles, within the self-characteristics and common characteristics of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases, employ the contemplations of suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self; because their minds of weary detachment from birth and death are so intense, they do not delight in practicing or drawing near to the objects of the six sense-fields.
To speak of "non-perverted vision" means to sever the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*).
For "delusive thoughts not to arise" means to sever the delusions of thought (*bhāvanā-kleśa*).
Since one has extinguished both suffering (*duḥkha*) and its accumulation (*samudaya*) to realize true emptiness (*śūnyatā*), it is said: "one conceives the realization of nirvāṇa therein."
"Furthermore, Mahāmati,
there are two kinds of characteristics of self-nature. What are the two?
These are: attachment to the characteristics of the intrinsic nature of verbal expression, and attachment to the characteristics of the intrinsic nature of things.
Attachment to the characteristics of the intrinsic nature of verbal expression arises from attachment to the habitual tendencies of beginningless false discourse.
"Attachment to the self-nature and characteristics of phenomena arises from the failure to realize that they are merely the manifestations of one's own mind.
As stated in the sutras, the two kinds of natures and characteristics arise each with their respective causes.
If one realizes that the nature of verbal expression is empty and that all phenomena are but mind, how could there be any conceptual attachment?
"Phenomena" refers precisely to all dharmas.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati!"

The Tathāgata establishes [them] through two kinds of spiritual powers (*ṛddhi*), whereby the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas prostrate to the Buddhas, listen to their teachings, and inquire about their meaning.
What are these two kinds of spiritual power by which they are established?
This refers to the power of manifesting all bodies, faces, and speech through the correct reception of samādhi, as well as the power of hand-consecration.
Regarding the establishment of these two kinds of spiritual power, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:
"The Buddhas possess two kinds of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) by which they sustain the bodhisattvas, causing them to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet and inquire about various meanings."

“Samādhi” is equivalent to “right reception” (*samyak-samāpatti*); this term combines both the Chinese and Sanskrit meanings, and it is also translated as “the sphere of right mental activity. “Mahāmati!
At the first bodhisattva stage, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva abides by the Buddha’s spiritual power, namely, entering the Bodhisattva Mahāyāna Illumination Samādhi.”

Having entered this samādhi, all the Buddhas of the worlds in the ten directions, through their supernormal powers, manifest for him all bodies, faces, and speech, just as they do for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha and other Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who have likewise accomplished such marks and virtues.

Regarding "abiding by the Buddha's spiritual power": it is through the Buddha's spiritual power that one is enabled to see the Buddha; furthermore, it is through the roots of goodness of the bodhisattva’s samādhi that a resonance and unification can be achieved. Therefore, it is called "entering the Mahāyāna Illumination Samādhi," which is the samādhi of radiance.
Because of this meditative concentration, one sees the Buddha and hears the Dharma.
As for the one like Vajragarbha, he is a bodhisattva who was empowered by the Buddha's power within the assembly of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra.
Using one case as an illustration for all others, it says "and the rest. "Mahāmati!
This is called the first stage of a bodhisattva."

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva attains the supernatural power of the Bodhisattva-samādhi-samāpatti, which has been accomplished through the accumulation of roots of goodness over hundreds of thousands of kalpas. Having thoroughly mastered the characteristics of the stages of practice—the antidotes and their objects—throughout the successive grounds, he reaches the ultimate stage of the Cloud of Dharma (Dharmameghā-bhūmi). There, he dwells in a subtle and wondrous palace of great lotuses, seated upon a great lotus jewel lion-throne, surrounded by a retinue of fellow Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, his body adorned with various precious necklaces, radiant like gold, campaka flowers, the sun, or the moon.

The most eminent hands come from the ten directions and bestow the consecration upon the crown of his head while he sits upon the throne of the Great Lotus Palace; it is like the consecration of a sovereign Wheel-Turning King or the Crown Prince of Śakra, Lord of Devas. This is called the Bodhisattva’s power of hand-consecration.
Mahāmati! These are called the two kinds of spiritual power of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva abides in these two kinds of spiritual power, they will behold the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, face to face.
"If it were not thus, one would be unable to see.
Regarding the phrase "in hundreds of thousands of kalpas," this clarifies the reason why Bodhisattvas of the first stage receive empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
The sequence of the various stages proceeds from shallow to deep.
This is like the reiteration of the matter of consecration (*abhiṣeka*) following the descent of Maheśvara.
"If one does not do so, one cannot see" is a summary that serves as a negative illustration (*pratibimba*).
"Furthermore, Mahāmati! [is said].

Whatever samādhis, bases of psychic power, and various dharmic practices the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas differentiate, all of these abide entirely within the two kinds of supernatural power of the Tathāgata.
Mahāmati!
If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas were able to expound and explain [the Dharma] apart from the Buddha’s spiritual power, then all ordinary worldlings should also be able to speak it. Why is this so?
This is because he does not abide in [limited] supernatural powers. Mahāmati!

Due to the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata’s entry into a city, mountains, stones, trees, musical instruments, city walls, and palaces all spontaneously produce the sounds of music; how much more so for sentient beings? Even those with immeasurable sufferings—such as the deaf, the blind, and the mute—all attain liberation. The Tathāgata possesses such immeasurable supernatural powers to benefit and bring peace to sentient beings.
The passage beginning with "All that is conceptually differentiated" further explains the meaning of being empowered [by the Buddha's power], establishing the intent of the subsequent analogy.

This means that all the dharmas, such as samādhis, which a bodhisattva expounds are entirely due to abiding in the Buddha’s supernatural power (*ṛddhi-bala*). Thus, by using the ordinary person as a contrast to the noble one, it is said that if a bodhisattva were separated from this supernatural power, they would be unable to say anything; how much more so, then, for an ordinary person?
If one attains supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), even insentient objects become functional; how much more so, then, could sentient beings not be liberated from suffering?
To say that ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) do not abide in supernormal powers is merely for the noble ones to surpass the ordinary.

Furthermore, as for the statement, "The Tathāgata possesses such supernatural powers," this means that within the Tathāgata’s Great Samādhi, there is stillness yet constant illumination; in accordance with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), he manifests myriad phenomena without anything being impossible, and yet how could there be any intentional effort involved therein?
The Bodhisattva Mahāmati addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“World-Honored One!

By what causes and conditions do the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas bestow their supernormal power upon Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas when they abide in the meditative absorptions (samāpatti) of the three times, and at the time of the empowerment (abhiṣeka) of the stages of advancement?”
The Buddha told Mahāmati:

"In order to bring about detachment from the afflictions of Māra’s activities, to prevent falling into the meditative states of the Śrāvaka stage, to attain the stage of the Tathāgata’s self-realization, and to further advance in the dharmas already attained—for these reasons, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas all establish the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas through their supernatural power."

If one does not establish oneself through spiritual power, then one will fall into the false views and delusive imaginings of the non-Buddhists, as well as the expectations of the śrāvakas and various māras, and shall fail to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"For this reason, all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, sustain all Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas through their supernatural powers.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The Honored One among Men, by his supernatural power, Has completely purified his great vows."
"The empowerment of samādhi, from the first stage to the tenth stage.
This section further asks why the Tathāgata bestows his grace upon bodhisattvas.
The Tathāgata answers with four meanings, as can be seen in the sūtra.

This is because a bodhisattva at the initial stage has not yet perfected the power of the Path; unless they receive the empowerment of the Tathāgata’s spiritual power, they can not only fail to advance to the stage of a Tathāgata, but will also be unable to distance themselves from the demonic realm of the śrāvakas.
The Tathāgata’s intention to embrace [beings] with compassion is indeed profound!
The verses are easily understood.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
When the Buddha speaks of dependent origination, he is speaking of causes and conditions; he does not speak of it as his own personal doctrine.
World-Honored One!”
The non-Buddhists also speak of causal conditions, asserting that all such natures arise from a Supreme Lord, Īśvara, Time, or atoms.
However, the Blessed One’s discourse on the arising of all natures through causal conditions consists of both the *siddhānta* with intervals and the *siddhānta* without intervals.

Regarding the discourse on causes and conditions, there are both the correct and the false; that which is taught by the Buddha is correct, while that taught by non-Buddhists is false. These two must be known, and for this reason, Mahāmati raised them together as a question.

"Not teaching one's own way" means that while the Buddha teaches dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), he does not speak of the underlying cause of dependent origination; therefore, it is called "not teaching one's own way.
The non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) claim that things arise from a supreme being, Īśvara, or other such causes, asserting that these various natures (*bhāva*) are themselves all phenomena (*dharma*).
However, is there a difference between this and the teachings on the dharma of dependent origination spoken by the Tathāgata for those of various capacities?
Or is there no difference?
The *siddhānta* is precisely the capacity of the four *siddhāntas*.
“World-Honored One!
The non-Buddhists also speak of existence, non-existence, and arising; the World-Honored One also speaks of non-arising and the cessation of what has arisen.

According to what the World-Honored One has taught—that ignorance conditions formations, and so on, up to old age and death—this is a teaching of causelessness by the World-Honored One, not a teaching of causality.”
The World-Honored One established this teaching, stating that "because this exists, that exists," rather than establishing a gradual arising.
This is because he observed that the assertions of the non-Buddhists were superior [in their logic], and not those of the Tathāgata.
Why is this so? World-Honored One!
The non-Buddhists speak of causes, asserting that there is something produced which does not arise from conditions.

“The World-Honored One has taught that by observing causes one finds effects, and by observing effects one finds causes; thus, these causes and conditions are intermingled, and in this manner they proceed in succession without end.

He also spoke of the arising from existence and non-existence: the outsiders claim that existence arises from non-existence, which would mean it is merely causeless; he also spoke of the non-arising of existence and so forth.

The Buddha said that there is no arising, and what has arisen has ceased, such as in the case of "ignorance conditions volitional formations" (*avidyā-pratyayāḥ saṃskārāḥ*). Is this not also saying that the Buddha taught there is no cause?

Below, the World-Honored One establishes [the principle] by means of the objection regarding confusion: the Buddha constantly says that "because this exists, that exists," which implies they exist simultaneously rather than being produced through a gradual sequence.
This is not merely a matter of parity; rather, it is seen that the teachings of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) are superior.
The causal principles of the non-Buddhists are indeed different causes; the Buddha’s teaching is distinct, such as [the principle] that there is an effect based on observing the cause.
Since they would exist mutually, confusion would ensue, resulting in the fallacy of an infinite regress.
These are all the objections raised by Mahāmati.
The Buddha said to Mahāmati:
“I do not speak without cause, nor do I speak with confused causes and conditions.
‘Because this exists, that exists’ refers to the non-existence of the grasper and the grasped, which is the realization that all is merely the manifestation of one’s own mind.”
Mahāmati!

If one is attached to the grasped and the grasper, failing to realize that external objects are merely the manifestation of one's own mind, and thus perceives the nature of external realms as either existent or non-existent, such a person incurs these faults; this is not what I call dependent origination.
"I have always said that all phenomena arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions; they do not arise without a cause.
In the response, he first refutes the opponent's objection in general, and subsequently explains his own correct meaning.

Regarding the statement "because this exists, that exists": "this" refers to the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*), and "that" refers to the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*; *ṣaḍāyatana*); it means that the faculties and objects arise in mutual dependence.

As for the phrase "the grasper and the grasped, the non-substantiality [of their nature]," etc., it means that one realizes that phenomena produced by causes and conditions are manifestations of mind alone, and thus lack the nature of a grasper (*grāhaka*) or a grasped (*grāhya*).
"Non-nature" (*abhāva*) refers to being free from the attachment to nature (*bhāva*).
Regarding such attachments as grasping at the grasper and the grasped, the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* states:

"If one does not understand that all phenomena are manifestations of mind-only, yet conceives of a grasper and a grasped, and clings to external objects as either existent or non-existent, such faults exist; these are not what I have taught."
"Transgression is precisely confusion; 'that' refers to the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas). 'Nature and non-nature' refers to existence and non-existence.

That which arises through the conjunction of causes and conditions is the direct response to the question regarding causelessness; how could it be the same as the heterodox and false notion of causelessness held by the non-Buddhists?"
Mahāmati spoke again to the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
is it not the case that because speech has existence, all things have existence?”
“World-Honored One!
If there were no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), speech would not arise; therefore, speech has an intrinsic nature, and all things have an intrinsic nature.

Because of the preceding discussion on phenomena arising through causes and conditions, he consequently doubted whether speech possesses an intrinsic nature and whether all dharmas likewise possess an intrinsic nature.
If all phenomena lack intrinsic nature, from what would speech arise?
Consequently, they form a misconception, saying: "Speech has intrinsic nature; all things have intrinsic nature.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
“Expressions are made regarding that which lacks intrinsic nature, such as ‘the horns of a rabbit’ or ‘the hair of a tortoise’; these are expressions commonly used in the world.
Mahāmati, it is neither existence nor non-existence; it is merely a verbal expression.”
"If it were as you say—that speech possesses an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and that all things possess an intrinsic nature—then your own thesis would be undermined.

The Buddha answered that while there is no intrinsic nature, speech nevertheless exists; he meant that although causes and conditions are fundamentally without intrinsic nature, this does not preclude their being indicated through speech. How could speech itself necessarily constitute an intrinsic nature?

As it is commonly said in the world regarding the hair of a tortoise, the horns of a rabbit, or the son of a barren woman—though these are fundamentally without intrinsic nature, yet they are spoken of—they are neither nature nor non-nature.

To say that it is not of the nature [of reality] means it is not real; yet, to say it is not non-existent means that verbal expression is not precluded. Therefore, it is said, "it is merely verbal expression.
The concluding censure, "your argument is destroyed," refers to the collapse of the doctrine that [things] possess both existence and non-existence.
“Mahāmati! It is not that all buddha-fields possess verbal expression; verbal expression is merely a fabrication. In some buddha-fields, the Dharma is revealed by gazing;

in some, by gestures; in some, by raising the eyebrows; in some, by moving the eyes; in some, by smiling; in some, by yawning; in some, by clearing the throat; in some, by mindfulness of the buddha-field; and in some, by shaking.”
Mahāmati!

It is as in the world-systems of Cakṣuḥprekṣaṇa and Gandhavyūha, and in the land of the Tathāgata Samantabhadra, where by mere gazing, all bodhisattvas are enabled to attain the realization of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) and various supreme samādhis.
Therefore, it is not that all things possess an intrinsic nature by virtue of verbal expression. Mahāmati!
Observe these beings in this world—mosquitoes, gnats, insects, and ants—who each accomplish their tasks without the use of speech.

"All lands and so forth" do not necessarily mean that every correct word is a verbal expression; rather, verbal expressions merely function in accordance with conditions. Since they act without acting, how could they possess an inherent nature?
There may be buddha-fields where the Dharma is manifested through gazing and so forth; these all accord with the capacities of beings, as the methods of transformation differ.

This is because the Buddhas' establishment of transformation does not rely exclusively on vocal instruction; fragrance, flavor, touch, and mental objects are all without exception the teachings of the sutras, and each can manifest the Dharma and lead one into the Way.

Just as practitioners of Chan employ the striking of the mallet, the raising of the whisk, the lifting of the eyebrows, or the twinkling of the eyes to receive students, it is likewise from this [source] that they emerge.
How narrow-minded it is for the world to regard only verbal discourse as the teaching!
Regarding "like one who gazes," this refers to the world of Animiṣa (the Unblinking); whereas previously it was merely indicated in general terms, here it is specified individually.

Just as in the world of Gandhavyūha (Fragrant Accumulation), where incense serves as the Buddha-work, one can infer that other sensory objects are likewise employed for edification; how much more so must this be the case for the transformations enacted by the Sages?

As for the subtle categories of sentient beings, there are also those who can accomplish their tasks without relying on verbal expression; thus it is said, "seeing the mosquitoes, gnats, insects, and ants of this world," and so forth.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Like space, a rabbit’s horns, And the son of a barren woman— Though they do not exist, there are words for them;
Such is the nature of deluded conceptualization."
"Phenomena produced by the harmony of causes and conditions / Are objects of deluded thought for the ignorant;
/ Unable to know them as they truly are, / They wander through the house of the three realms of existence.
As for the term "son of Paṇḍu," it refers to the son of a barren woman.

The hare’s horn and other such examples all serve as metaphors for that which is fundamentally non-existent yet expressed through verbal designation; likewise, although phenomena are fundamentally without intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), they are conceptually imagined to have a nature. Therefore, it is said: “Such is the conceptualization of nature.”

By way of analogy, because ordinary, ignorant people cannot know, through their false imaginings, the nature of dharmas as they arise from causes and conditions, there exists the phenomenon of saṃsāra within the three realms of existence.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"What does the 'eternal sound' refer to?
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"It refers to delusive confusion; yet because of that delusive confusion, even the noble ones manifest it, though it is not a perversion."
Mahāmati!

Just as a springtime mirage, a whirling firebrand, falling hair, a city of the Gandharvas, a phantom, a dream, and a reflection in a mirror are misconceptions of the world and not the domain of the wise, yet they are nonetheless manifest.
Mahāmati! That delusion manifests in various ways; it is not that the delusion itself creates impermanence. Why is this so?
This means that it is because of being free from both existence and non-existence.
Regarding the term "eternal" (*nitya*), it refers to the teaching of eternal dharmas.
The intent of the question is: upon what basis does the Tathāgata teach these eternal dharmas?
"Delusion" refers to impermanence; the Buddha’s intention is precisely that he speaks of permanence regarding what is impermanent, because one must realize that impermanence is itself permanence.

As for the statement that "the sages also manifest it," this means that the phenomena of delusive impermanence and birth-and-death are not created solely by sentient beings in reality, but are also provisionally manifested by the Buddhas after their fruition to show themselves as being the same as sentient beings. This is done so that they may understand that impermanence is itself permanence; since they do not act like ordinary worldlings, it is said that they are "not inverted."

The seven similes, such as the springtime mirage and others, precisely illustrate the confusion of inverted delusions; ordinary beings remain lost in ignorance, grasping at what is non-existent as existent and perceiving the impermanent as permanent—this constitutes inversion.
Although this is not the concern of the wise, it is nonetheless not unmanifest.

Furthermore, he tells Mahāmati: regarding that "delusion" and so forth, this means that when those false phenomena appear, although they possess various distinct differences, they are not impermanent.
This is because all dharmas are fundamentally detached from existence and non-existence; each and every one is the very nature (dharmatā). Because they are the nature, they are eternal.
To be detached from both nature and non-nature is precisely to be detached from existence and non-existence.
“Mahāmati! What is the delusion that is free from existence and non-existence?
It refers to the various objective realms of all foolish commoners.”
Just as with that Ganges River, because hungry ghosts do not see it, it lacks the nature of delusion; yet, because it appears to others, it is not without nature.
In this way, for the noble ones who are free from both inversion and non-inversion, delusion is eternal, because its characteristics are never destroyed.
"Mahāmati! It is not that the various marks of delusion (*bhrānti*) are destroyed by the marks of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); therefore, delusion is eternal.

Regarding the passage beginning with "How so?"—it means that although the nature of the phenomena of delusion is fundamentally eternal as seen by the sages, they must say it is "devoid of both existence and non-existence" because ordinary people have not yet attained realization; such is the realm of the foolish.

Regarding the phrase "like that Ganges River and so forth," this takes up what is seen by the foolish as a metaphor: although the hungry ghosts are near the Ganges, they do not see water; because they perceive the water as fire, it is said that they "see yet do not see."
Although there are differences in perception, the substance of that Ganges remains as it always has been.

Regarding "the absence of a nature of delusive confusion," this means that one does not posit existence based on seeing, nor does one posit non-existence based on not seeing; from the perspective of the one who sees, the Ganges is not non-existent. Therefore, it is said: "Because it appears to others, it is not of a non-existent nature."

Regarding such delusions and the like, this correctly explains the meaning of the permanence of delusion: because the noble ones are free from both inverted and non-inverted views, the very essence of that delusion is eternally abiding, for its dharmas are indestructible.

Furthermore, as for the statement that it is "not delusive," this means that the various false dharmas do not themselves possess diverse and distinct characteristics; rather, it is through the conceptual discrimination of ignorant people that these differing characteristics are perceived.
If one is free from conceptual discrimination, delusive phenomena are eternal; therefore, it is said that confusion is eternal.
"Mahāmati! What is the reality of confusion?"
Furthermore, Mahāmati, regarding these delusions, the noble ones do not give rise to perverted cognition, nor is it a case of non-perverted cognition.
With the exception of the noble ones, all others possess some degree of conceptualization regarding these delusions; they are not the objective phenomena of noble wisdom.
"Mahāmati!
That which exists is a false assertion by the ignorant; it is not the teaching of the noble ones.
Thus says the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*:
"How does one attain the reality of illusory phenomena?
It means that the noble ones do not give rise to either perverted or non-perverted cognitions regarding illusory phenomena.
If there were even the slightest conceptualization toward illusory phenomena, it would not be noble wisdom."
"One who possesses even slight conceptualization should be known as a fool engaged in frivolous proliferation; this is not the discourse of the noble ones.
That delusion consists of inverted and non-inverted false imaginings, which give rise to two kinds of natures:
namely, the nature of the noble ones and the nature of fools."
The noble lineage is distinguished into three types: namely, the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the Buddha vehicle.
How does the deluded thought of an ordinary person give rise to the lineage of the Śrāvaka vehicle?

This refers to the attachment to specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), which gives rise to the lineage of the Śrāvaka vehicle; this is called the arising of the lineage of the Śrāvaka vehicle from delusive thought.

Mahāmati! That very same delusive thought, when it arises from non-intimate attachment to the specific and general characteristics of that same confusion, gives rise to the lineage of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle. This is called the arising of the lineage of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle from delusive thought.
How does the wise one give rise to the lineage of the Buddha-vehicle from within that very delusion?

It means that by awakening to the fact that all is merely the manifestation of one's own mind, and that external natures have no inherent existence, one ceases to conceptualize the marks of phenomena; thus giving rise to the lineage of the Buddha-vehicle is called "giving rise to the lineage of the Buddha-vehicle from within that very delusion."
Regarding the statement "that which is delusive," this refers to the discrimination of false dharmas as either inverted or non-inverted, thereby establishing two distinct natures:
the non-inverted is the noble one, while the inverted is the foolish commoner.
First, regarding the emergence of the noble lineage, there are further three types: namely, the Śrāvaka, Pratyekabuddha, and Buddha vehicles.

Within the initial Śrāvaka vehicle, the statement that "the delusions of foolish people arise" means that when foolish people clearly perceive the self-characteristics and common characteristics of the five aggregates as empty and quiescent, they give rise to weary detachment, thereby forming the Śrāvaka lineage.

Regarding the term "self-characteristics and common characteristics" used for pratyekabuddhas: while their meaning is identical to that of "detachment from grasping," they are said to be "unfamiliar" because they delight in cultivating seclusion; this constitutes the lineage of the pratyekabuddha.

Within the Buddha-lineage, the term "the wise" is specifically used to distinguish them from the two vehicles; the meaning of "realizing that all is the manifestation of one's own mind" and so forth has been explained previously—this constitutes the Buddha-vehicle lineage.
Furthermore, the nature of various phenomena is a deluded conception of ordinary people, which gives rise to the lineage of the foolish.
That is neither an existent thing nor a non-existent thing; this is called the meaning of "lineage" (gotra).
Mahāmati!

That very delusion which is non-conceptual—the transformation of the nature of dharmas through the habit-energies of the mind, intellect, and consciousness of the noble ones—is called "suchness. Therefore, it is said that suchness is free from the mind.
When I speak this phrase to reveal the departure from conceptualization, I mean the departure from all conceptualizations.

Within the lineage of the foolish, that which is called the "nature of various things" refers to the discrimination of various phenomena and objects; by adhering to these objects according to their appearances, one establishes their nature.

Regarding the statement that "those are not entities," etc., it means that those very delusive phenomena are neither entities nor non-entities; they are neither existent nor non-existent, and this constitutes the lineage of the ignorant.

Furthermore, the statement "that very delusion is non-conceptualization" reiterates the lineage of the Buddha-vehicle (*buddhayāna-gotra*). It indicates that it is not merely a matter of not conceptualizing false phenomena; rather, one must undergo a complete transformation of all factors such as the afflictions of mind, intellect, and consciousness (*citta-manovijñāna*), as well as their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). When this transformation reaches its ultimate limit, one returns to one's original nature, wherein everything is nothing other than the single Suchness (*tathatā*). Because all things are thus, one is free from the mind and transcends conceptual thought.
This phrase is the phrase of transcending the mind and severing conceptualization; it refers to what was previously called "True Suchness free from thought," which is the severance of the mind.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!"
"Is delusion existent or non-existent?
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"It is like a magical illusion; it has no characteristics to which one should cling."

"If delusive confusion possessed the characteristic of attachment, then the nature of that attachment could not be extinguished, and dependent origination would be like the 'dharmas produced by causes and conditions' as described by the non-Buddhists.
From this point downward, there are four questions and answers:

first, the question regarding whether delusive confusion exists or not; based on the preceding discussion, [it was argued] that delusive confusion is permanent and real, yet it is also considered a false imagination—therefore, does the fruit exist?
"Is the fruit non-existent?

The Buddha answered that it is like an illusion and devoid of any characteristic of conceptual attachment; his intention was that if one were to say that delusive dharmas definitely exist or definitely do not exist, then the nature of conceptual attachment would arise and could not be extinguished. Therefore, he spoke of them as being like illusions.

If one cannot comprehend that [all things] are like an illusion, then the phenomena of dependent origination would be identical to the false conceptualizations regarding causes and conditions held by non-Buddhists.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!"
"If delusive confusion were like an illusion, it would further act as a cause for other delusions.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"Illusion is not the cause of delusion, because it does not give rise to faults."
Mahāmati!
An illusion does not give rise to faults, for it is devoid of conceptual construction. Mahāmati!
An illusion arises from the power of another's clarity, not from the habitual tendencies of one's own deluded conceptualizations; therefore, it does not give rise to faults.
Mahāmati, this is merely the attachment of the deluded minds of the foolish, not that of the noble ones.
This question arises from the answer.
If delusion is like an illusion, can it further give rise to faults, acting as a cause for other delusions to produce dharmas?
The Buddha replied that "illusion is not a cause of delusion," for three reasons:
first, because illusion does not give rise to faults; second, because it is devoid of false conceptualization; and third, because it arises from a source of clarity.
Regarding the fields of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*), the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:
"A vidyā-mantra refers to an illusion produced from incantations and ritual arts; it does not arise from the habitual tendencies of one's own conceptual discrimination."

However, these three meanings all clarify that illusions do not give rise to evil and are not the cause of delusive phenomena; rather, it is when one discriminates and gives rise to the faults of delusive confusion that one becomes an ordinary person (pṛthagjana), and thus it is said they are not sages or worthies.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
The Noble Ones do not perceive delusion, Nor is there any reality in the interval between.
If the interval were truly real, Then delusion would itself be reality.
"Having abandoned all delusions, if any signs of arising should appear, these too are delusive confusion; they are impure, like a cataract.

The first four lines clarify that the noble wisdom of the Mahāyāna realizes that the false is itself the true. Delusive confusion and false phenomena are the domain of ordinary beings; when seen with the Buddha-eye, there is nothing that is not reality.

Furthermore, this reality is not a substantial entity; rather, that which is free from both emptiness and existence is reality, for it is precisely because noble wisdom realizes that delusive phenomena are themselves reality.
The final four lines clarify that even those of small wisdom who have abandoned delusion to reveal the truth may still become confused and disturbed by clinging to signs within that very truth;
it is like having a cataract in the eye, whereby one perceives things as impure.
Commentary on the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, Fascicle Two, Part One.
